processinfo.head: Processing Information

p.emph: Starting in 2023, Library of Virginia archival staff in partnership with the Virginia Untold Project Manager began efforts to describe records related to free and enslaved Black and multiracial people in a manner that improved the historical context of the records. In doing so, in some cases material once described within the "Free and Enslaved" record group for a locality may no longer be described within this record. When this has occurred, please see the Processing Information and Related Materials section for records that have been described separately.

processinfo.p: These records have been processed, scanned, and indexed by LVA staff for the purposes of digitizing them for the digital project Virginia Untold: The African American Narrative.
Certificates of Importation were removed from this record in August 2026 and are now described in Henry County (Va.) Certificates of Importation.
"Free Negro" Registrations were removed from this record in August 2026 and are now described in Henry County (Va.) Records related to the Registration of Free Persons.

Agreements of Edmund Randolph and Ephraim Volintine and other records related to the Freemen's Bureau were removed from this record in August 2026 and are now described in Henry County (Va.) Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands Records
A photocopy of judgment case Commonwealth vs. Henry Harris, a free negro, for having an illegal firearm (1850 May) was not located during redescription in August 2026.
Encoded by S. Nerney, 2007; Updated by M. Mason August 2026

bioghist.head: Historical Information
bioghist.p: The Free and Enslaved Records collection is comprised of miscellaneous records related to the regulation and policing of both enslaved and free Black and Multiracial people in Bedford County. The localities/local government authorities were largely responsible for enforcing laws that restricted the movement of enslaved and free Black and Multiracial people and the resulting documentation was often filed in the circuit courts. The ways in which local authorities enacted legal measures against or on behalf of enslaved and free Black and Multiracial people varied from locality to locality; therefore, records were not necessarily standardized or filed and retained in a consistent manner. This collection is topical and a means by which to compile miscellaneous documents related to free and enslaved people that are not established local government record types.
See: the Virginia Untold Record Types on the Library of Virginia website for additional context concerning "Free Negro" Tax Records and "Runaway" records

Locality History:Henry County like Patrick County, was named for Patrick Henry, who was the first governor of the commonwealth of Virginia. It was formed from Pittsylvania County in 1776. The county court first met on 20 January 1777. Part of Patrick County was added later in 1858.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Content
scopecontent.p: Henry County (Va.) Free and Enslaved Records, 1796-1865,undated, contains "Free Negro" Tax records, 1842-1862, undated; Patrol Records, 1796-1863, undated; Requisitions for Public Use, 1862-1865, undated; and various record types, 1853-1860, undated.

"Free Negro" Tax records, 1842-1862, consists of fifteen "Lists of Free Negroes," 1842,1844-1847,1849-1852,1855,1857,1860,1862, undated which were compiled by the commissioner of the revenue for tax purposes. The lists give the full name, sex, and trade or occupation for each person on the list. Some lists additionally indicate age and residence. The 1852 list is a fragment. [Digitized]

Patrol Records, 1796-1863, undated, of which these patrols generally acted as the policing force that monitored the movement of free and enslaved Black and Multiracial individuals. These record the names of the individuals on patrol; who authorized their patrol; dates of patrol; the number of hours on patrol; general geographic area patrolled; and compensation awarded. Some returns specifically note the objective to "apprehend all slaves and other disorderly persons," or "to visit all negro quarters, and other places suspected of entertaining unlawful assemblies of servants, slaves, or of disorderly persons." The captain of the patrol is usually indicated. The patrol orders and appointments are directives by the justice of the peace for specifically named men to patrol the county for a specific amount of time. [Not digitized]

Requisitions for Public Use, 1862-1865, undated, contain various lists and receipts related to the requisition of free and enslaved Black and Multiracial people to work on the fortifications during the Civil War. Records include lists of enslavers and the number of enslaved individuals sent; lists of enslavers and named enslaved persons sent to the public works; orders from the state or county government regarding the requisitions; lists of free Black and Multiracial people drafted into work; a "list of hands hired for the government stables"; a receipt for providing meals to "negroes"; and a list of enslaved individuals examined by the medical board which notes enslaved person's name, their enslaver, age, and whether they are fit for work or exempt for a medical reason. [Only records containing named enslaved people are digitized]

Additional documentation regarding Black and Multiracial individuals exists on microfilm Henry County (Va.) Reel 104 and Miscellaneous Reel 1134. Henry County (Va.) Reel 104 contains record of births and deaths from December 1852 to December 1853 which includes notes about enslaved people. Miscellaneous Reel 1134 contains public records relating to Black individuals, 1867-1900, and public records relating to enslaved Black persons, 1858-1866. These public records appear to be photocopies of minute book entries involving Black or enslaved people and then in the margin, someone's notes about mentions of "Black citizens" and enslaved people.
Additional items relating to the documentation of free and enslaved Black and multiracial individuals in and around Henry County, Va., include:
An appointment, undated, for justice of oyer and terminer

Lists,1853-1860, of enslaved persons held by the dower estates of Kittura Cole, Ruth S. Hairston, and Martha H. Perkins. These list note name of the person who holds the enslaved people, the names and sometimes the ages of the enslaved people, and the former enslaver or potential enslaver. [Digitized] Enslaved persons named in the Kittura Cole estate: Matilda, Catherine, Jesse, Matilda, Anity, Caroline, Will, Jem, Usley, William, Caroline. Ruth S. Hairston estate: Peyton, Solomon, Dennis, Susan, Becky, Jane, Tom, Holbrooke, Cornelia, Tom, Isbel, Issac, Joe, Daniel, Perry, Tip, Betsy, Nelly, Esther, Lucy, Theny, Dillard, Murry, Betty, Joe, Thenia, Betsy, Daniel . Martha H. Perkins: Milly: Thom, Winston, Millor, Flora, Elizabeth, Maiz, Grace, Sarah, Margarett, Jassup (Joseph), Samuel, Jim, Mily, Kiziah, Mary, Lucy, Maria. Report for hire, 1855, of Eliza, a Black woman enslaved by Elizabeth Jones, along with Eliza's children Mary Janes, and Martha. [Digitized]

Summons, 1855, 1859, includes seven summonses, 1855, of the court for witnesses to speak on behalf of George L. Baker, a man of "mixed blood" in regard to his application to certify "that he is not a negro."; and six summonses, 1859, of the court for witnesses to speak on behalf of George W. Baker, Jeffery Eskhols, and Jefferson Key, men of "mixed blood" applying to certify that they are "not a negro." [Digitized]
Summons, 1860, in judgment Harris vs. Brewer concerning the rescinding of an apprenticeship indenture of Joseph Harris bonded out to John D. Brewer, due to failure to comply with the covenants.
